questions.stem: A banking portal requires a password, then a PIN, then the answer to a security question. How should this be described?
options: Three-factor authentication, since three separate secrets are required
Single-factor authentication, since all three are Type 1 "something you know"
Two-factor authentication, since the PIN and the security question form one factor together
Multi-factor authentication, since the number of challenges exceeds two
questions.explanation: MFA requires factors from different types, not more challenges of the same type. All three are knowledge-based, so a single phishing page or credential dump defeats all of them at once. This is the most reliably tested idea in the whole domain.

questions.stem: A bank is tuning the biometric readers used for vault access. Which error rate should it prioritise reducing, and why?
options: FRR, because rejected staff will find workarounds that undermine the control
Neither — the CER is fixed by the hardware and cannot be tuned
FRR, because it is the Type II error and represents the security failure
FAR, because it is the Type II error and admits impostors
questions.explanation: False Acceptance is the security failure; false rejection is only an inconvenience. (C) is the deliberate mix — it names the right reasoning but attaches it to the wrong rate. (A) describes a real operational risk, which makes it tempting, but a bank vault will always accept friction over impostors.

questions.stem: Two fingerprint readers are being compared for accuracy. Reader X has a CER of 1.8%; reader Y has a CER of 3.1%. Which is more accurate, and what does CER represent?
options: Reader X — CER is the point at which FAR equals FRR, and a lower value indicates a more accurate device
Reader Y — a higher CER indicates greater sensitivity and therefore better detection
Reader X — CER is the combined total of FAR and FRR at the default setting
Neither can be judged without knowing the FAR and FRR separately
questions.explanation: The crossover rate is the standard single-figure comparison, and lower is better. (C) gets the direction right but the definition wrong — CER is the crossover point, not a sum. (D) is the cautious-sounding answer that would be correct for many comparisons but not this one; CER exists precisely so a single comparison is possible.

questions.stem: Which statement about SSO and MFA is correct?
options: SSO is a form of MFA in which the second factor is the existing session
Deploying SSO removes the need for MFA, since there is only one login to protect
SSO reduces the number of authentication events; MFA strengthens each one — SSO concentrates risk, so it increases rather than removes the need for MFA
MFA and SSO are incompatible, because MFA requires a fresh challenge at every system
questions.explanation: They solve different problems and are complementary. (B) is the dangerous misconception — a single compromised SSO credential now opens every connected system, which is exactly why strong, ideally phishing-resistant MFA belongs in front of it.

questions.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: OAuth 2.0 provides authentication; OpenID Connect provides encryption of the assertion
OAuth 2.0 provides delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds an authentication layer on top of it
OpenID Connect provides delegated authorization; OAuth 2.0 adds authentication
Both provide authentication, differing only in the transport used
questions.explanation: OAuth answers "may this application act on the user's behalf?"; OIDC answers "who is this user?". (C) is the straight inversion and the most common wrong choice. Treating an OAuth token as proof of identity is a real and recurring implementation flaw.

questions.stem: What does federation provide that conventional SSO within a single domain does not?
options: Trusted identity assertion across organisational boundaries, so a user authenticated by their own identity provider can access another organisation's services without a separate account
A stronger authentication factor, since federated protocols mandate MFA
Local storage of partner credentials, so that access survives a network outage
Automatic provisioning of accounts, which SSO cannot perform
questions.explanation: The defining feature is the trust relationship between organisations, with an IdP asserting identity to a relying service provider. (C) states the opposite of the design goal — federation exists so the service provider never holds the credential. (D) confuses federation with SCIM provisioning.

questions.stem: Which statement about biometric authentication is a genuine limitation rather than a myth?
options: Biometrics cannot be used as part of a multi-factor scheme
Biometric templates are stored as reversible images of the trait
Biometric readers cannot be tuned once installed
A compromised biometric cannot be reissued, unlike a password or a token
questions.explanation: You can rotate a password and replace a token; you cannot issue someone new fingerprints. This is why biometrics are best used as one factor and why template protection matters. (B) is false for well-designed systems, which store a mathematical template rather than an image.

questions.stem: A user types their username at a login prompt. Which step of the access chain has occurred?
options: Authentication, because the system now has a credential to evaluate
Authorization, because the username determines their permissions
Identification — the user has claimed an identity, which has not yet been proven
Accounting, because the attempt is recorded in the authentication log
questions.explanation: Identification is the claim; authentication is the proof. Collapsing the two is the classic error, and the distinction matters because a claimed identity carries no trust — usernames are frequently public.

questions.stem: What is the strongest design for provisioning new staff accounts?
options: Manual creation by the service desk on receipt of an email from the hiring manager
Automated provisioning triggered by the HR system as the authoritative source, granting role-based entitlements approved by the data owner
Cloning the account of an existing team member in the same role
Creating a standard account with broad access, to be narrowed at the first access review
questions.explanation: An authoritative source, role-based entitlements and owner approval make provisioning consistent, reviewable and auditable. (C) is the widespread real-world shortcut that propagates privilege creep from one account to the next, permanently. (D) inverts least privilege.

questions.stem: An analyst who moved from Payroll to Marketing eighteen months ago still holds access to the payroll system. What is this called, and which lifecycle activity should have caught it?
options: Privilege creep — a periodic access review or recertification should have identified and removed it
An orphaned account — deprovisioning should have removed it at the point of transfer
Excessive provisioning — the fault lies with the original account creation
Separation of duties failure — the analyst should never have held both roles
questions.explanation: Movers are riskier than joiners or leavers, because nothing forces a review at transfer. (B) is wrong on the definition: an orphaned account is one whose owner has left the organisation entirely, whereas this user is still employed.

questions.stem: An employee is to be terminated at 2 pm today. What is the correct first technical action, and when?
options: Delete the user account immediately after the meeting concludes
Change the user's password and leave the account active for handover
Disable the account as the exit conversation begins, before the employee returns to their desk
Wait 24 hours to allow the employee to forward outstanding work
questions.explanation: Access is removed at the moment the person learns their employment is ending — the window between notification and revocation is where data exfiltration and sabotage occur. (B) leaves active sessions and tokens intact; (D) is the well-intentioned answer that creates the largest risk window.

questions.stem: Why should a departing employee's account be disabled and archived rather than deleted immediately?
options: Because licensing agreements require dormant accounts to be retained for a fixed period
Because a disabled account continues to receive security patches
Because deletion would prevent the employee from being rehired later
Because deletion destroys audit history and potential evidence, and can orphan ownership of files and resources
questions.explanation: Disable first, delete later per the retention policy. Immediate deletion has repeatedly frustrated investigations — the account you delete on Friday is the one the forensic team needs on Monday. (A) and (B) are invented rationales that sound administratively plausible.

questions.stem: What is an orphaned account, and why is it a significant risk?
options: An account with more privileges than its role requires, creating an oversized blast radius
An account whose owner has left the organisation but which remains active — nobody monitors it, so its misuse is unlikely to be noticed
An account that has never been used since creation and can safely be ignored
A service account without an assigned password rotation schedule
questions.explanation: The defining risk is the absence of an owner who would notice misuse. (A) describes excessive privilege and (D) a service-account hygiene failure — both real problems, neither the definition. (C) contains the dangerous claim: dormant accounts are attractive precisely because activity on them raises no expectations.

questions.stem: In access governance, who decides which roles may access a given dataset, and who implements that decision?
options: The data owner decides; the data custodian implements
The data custodian decides; the system owner implements
The security team decides; the data owner implements
The data steward decides; the data processor implements
questions.explanation: The owner is the senior accountable person who classifies the data and approves access; the custodian is the day-to-day IT role that configures and maintains the protection. (C) is a common real-world drift — security advises and enforces policy, but does not own the business decision about who needs the data.

questions.stem: Which combination best manages standing administrative access?
options: Issuing every administrator a permanent second account with domain admin rights
Sharing a single administrator credential recorded in the team's password manager
Privileged access management with credential vaulting, session recording and just-in-time elevation that expires automatically
Granting administrative rights to the daily-use account but requiring a written justification afterwards
questions.explanation: Time-bounding the privilege is what shrinks the window of exposure; vaulting and session recording provide accountability. (A) is better than (D) but still leaves standing privilege permanently available. (B) destroys attribution entirely — shared accounts make accounting impossible.

questions.stem: Under the 2026 outline, how should an AI agent that calls internal APIs be treated?
options: As infrastructure, governed by change management rather than identity management
As an extension of the identity of whichever user invoked it
As exempt from access reviews, since its permissions are set programmatically
As an identity subject to the full life cycle — roles definition, provisioning, periodic review and deprovisioning — constrained by least privilege and separation of duties
questions.explanation: The outline is explicit that AI "bots" and automated service accounts go through formal identity life cycle management. (B) is the seductive one because it describes delegated authorization, which is sometimes appropriate — but an agent that acts autonomously needs its own reviewable identity and its own least-privilege entitlements.

questions.topic: Least privilege and separation of duties
questions.stem: A finance system is configured so that the person who raises a payment cannot also approve it. Which principle is this, and what does it defeat?
options: Least privilege — it limits what any single user is able to do
Separation of duties — it means fraud requires collusion between two people
Dual control — it requires two people to act at the same moment
Need to know — it restricts each user to the payment records relevant to their work
questions.explanation: SoD splits a sensitive process across people so no one can complete it alone. (C) is the closest miss and worth nailing down: dual control requires two people acting simultaneously on the same task (two keys, one launch), whereas SoD only requires that different people perform different steps at different times.

questions.topic: Least privilege and separation of duties
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes least privilege from separation of duties?
options: Least privilege applies to human users; separation of duties applies to service accounts
They are the same principle, with SoD being the term used in financial contexts
Least privilege limits how much one subject can do; separation of duties splits a process between subjects
Least privilege is a technical control; separation of duties is a physical control
questions.explanation: One is about the size of a single subject's entitlement; the other is about the shape of a process across several subjects. They are complementary — an over-privileged single account defeats SoD, because that one account can now perform every step.

questions.topic: Least privilege and separation of duties
questions.stem: Which administrative control is specifically designed to surface concealed fraud by ensuring another person performs a role while its usual holder is absent?
options: Mandatory vacation
Job rotation
Dual control
Least privilege
questions.explanation: Mandatory vacation — The mechanism is enforced absence: ongoing fraud usually requires continuous concealment, so irregularities surface when someone else covers the desk. (B) is the near-miss — job rotation achieves a similar detective effect over a longer horizon and also spreads skills, but it is not defined by enforced absence.

questions.topic: Least privilege and separation of duties
questions.stem: A cryptographic key ceremony requires two custodians to present their key shares at the same time before the master key can be assembled. Which control is this?
options: Separation of duties, since two people are involved
Job rotation, since custodianship alternates between staff
Least privilege, since neither custodian holds the whole key
Dual control, since two people must act simultaneously on the same task
questions.explanation: The simultaneity is the distinguishing feature. (A) is the trap for anyone who reads "two people" and stops — SoD divides different steps of a process; dual control requires two people on the same step at the same time. (C) describes a genuine side effect of split knowledge, but not the control being named.

questions.stem: On a shared file server, the creator of each folder can grant other users read or write access at their own discretion. Which model is in use?
options: MAC
RBAC
DAC
ABAC
questions.explanation: DAC — The giveaway is owner discretion — D for Discretion of the owner. This is the model behind standard Windows and Unix file permissions. It is flexible and it is the least restrictive, which is why it scales poorly and leaks access over time.

questions.stem: A defence system labels every document with a classification, assigns every user a clearance, and prevents document creators from sharing outside those labels regardless of their wishes. Which model?
options: DAC
MAC
RuBAC
RBAC
questions.explanation: MAC — Labels plus clearances plus no owner override is the definition, and it is the most restrictive model. The phrase "regardless of their wishes" is doing the work here — the moment an owner can override, you are looking at DAC.

questions.stem: Access to a records system is granted only when the requester is in the Clinical department, on a managed device, inside the hospital network, during a rostered shift. Which model?
options: ABAC
RBAC
MAC
RuBAC
questions.explanation: ABAC — Multiple attributes of subject, object and environment combined by policy — the most granular and context-aware model. (B) is the near-miss: role is only one of the four attributes here, and a pure RBAC decision would stop at "Clinical department".

questions.stem: Which comparison of the access control models is correct?
options: DAC is the most restrictive; ABAC is the least granular
RBAC is the most restrictive; MAC scales best in large organisations
MAC is the most restrictive; RBAC scales best for large organisations; ABAC is the most granular
RuBAC is the most granular, since rules can be written to any level of detail
questions.explanation: Worth memorising as a single line. (D) is the strongest distractor because it sounds reasonable — but RuBAC rules apply uniformly to everyone and do not evaluate subject attributes, which is precisely the granularity ABAC adds.

questions.stem: A firewall ruleset ends with a rule dropping all traffic not matched by a preceding rule. What is this posture called, and why is it preferred?
options: Fail-open, because it preserves availability when the ruleset is incomplete
Least privilege, since it grants the minimum bandwidth required
Defence in depth, since it forms an additional layer behind the earlier rules
Implicit deny — anything not explicitly permitted is refused, so a gap in the ruleset fails closed rather than exposing a service
questions.explanation: The security value is what happens to the case nobody anticipated: with implicit deny, an unforeseen protocol is blocked by default. (A) names the opposite behaviour. (B) misapplies a real principle — least privilege is about entitlements, not bandwidth.
